newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Some storm-hit Argentine wheat said to end as feed.
newsitem.headline: Some storm-hit Argentine wheat said to end as feed.

text.p: A portion of the wheat from the large area of Argentina's southern wheat belt battered by storms last week has sprouted and may have to be sold as feed wheat, analysts said Monday.

As government inspectors worked in sodden fields to assess how much damage had been done to what was headed to be a hefty wheat crop, crop watchers 600 miles (1,000 km) north in Buenos Aires tried to piece together what happened.
But while some analysts said they were concerned about possible significant damage, exporters dismissed talk that the crop was no longer bumper as farmer propaganda designed to push up prices.

"I would say that there is volume damage and there is quality damage. How much of each is something we'll end up knowing only when the combines get in, and no one knows when that will happen," one analyst told Reuters.

He said a fair proportion of crops in the affected area of southern Buenos Aires had sprouted on the head, rendering the grain useless for bread and fit only for feed. He added that there were reports that an area as high as 1.57 million hectares had been hit by the storms.

"This doesn't involve all the crop, but one thing is certain. If someone was thinking of buying good quality Argentine wheat, he now has to assume there'll be less good quality wheat. There'll also be some Argentine feeding wheat to sell, but it's not clear how much."
Farmers sowed 6.9 million hectares of 1996/97 wheat, about two-thirds of it in Buenos Aires province.

But a trader recently back from a southern crop tour said that reports of damage were alarmist: "I walked through fields in San Cayetano, Dorrego, Necochea, Balcarce. I didn't make it to where they say the worst damage was, near Bahia Blanca and La Pampa, but what I saw was spectacular wheat.

"What's happening here is that the producers are long by at least 12 million tonnes," he said, "We still think the harvest is going to be 16 million tonnes and there's going to be a lot of harvest pressure on prices at the end of December and the beginning of January.
He said he thought at most that about 400,000 tonnes of wheat had sprouted. "The rain has been better for the soybeans and the maize than it has been bad for the wheat."
But a second analyst said he had heard that around a fifth of the wheat in the rain-lashed area had sprouted.

Argentina's main farm lobby, the Rural Society, warned of a "climatic catastrophe" last Friday. The government's Agricultural Secretariat said it was preparing a rigorous damage report but no official was available for comment Monday.
Argentina's Meteorological Service forecast cloudy weather for southwest Buenos Aires and La Pampa Monday.
